We employ exact diagonalization to examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal structure, characteristic of transition metal oxides. By directly comparing with $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only models based on electron filling, we investigate the magnetic properties of all possible 3d, 4d, and 5d transition metal ions. The extent of $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing varies significantly among the series from 3d to 5d, influenced by the interplay between spin-orbit coupling, electron-electron repulsion, and crystal field splitting. As a result, the magnitude of $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can either be sufficiently small (less than 0.1 eV) to justify separate $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ descriptions for most heavier ions, or substantial enough (up to 0.5 eV) to necessitate a combined $t_{2g}$+$e_g$ treatment for some lighter ions. Notably, the heavier ions (especially 5d ions) exhibit a unique mixing phenomenon, where the energy minimum shifts from the $t_{2g}$ manifold to the $e_g$ manifold due to the dominant effect of electron-electron repulsion over spin-orbit coupling. This research has important implications

This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW.

Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged. This study explores the potential of using conditional GANs to manipulate medical images, specifically using a COVID-19-aware generator to modify chest X-rays containing the COVID-19 virus. By training the model on a vast dataset consisting of 480k X-ray images with associated metadata, including COVID-19 presence, our analysis reveals that the disease-aware generator can accurately capture subtle differences in chest X-rays and reproduce these patterns during the editing process. When tested on a separate dataset containing 10k X-ray images with COVID-19 presence labels, our results show that the model can successfully remove COVID-19 from modified images, as confirmed by both human observers and AI models. This innovative approach has far-reaching implications for medical imaging diagnostics, demonstrating the possibility of using AI to rectify low-quality medical images and improve accurate disease detection.

ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include
numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical methods such as weighted PCA, elastic maps, and
L1-based linear and multilinear techniques. It also enables the creation of
multiple types of visualizations, including 2D and 3D graphs, heat maps, and
scatter plots, as well as nonlinear visualization through UMAP and Holoview.
Additionally, it facilitates the execution of complex queries with a built-in
query language and a user interface for query development.

Evaluating Newtonian potentials over complex two-dimensional regions efficiently is crucial for solving Poisson's equation and volume integral equations numerically. For domains with irregular boundaries, using a grid without a set pattern to calculate the potential by splitting it into small areas becomes impractical due to high computational costs. In this paper, we propose an efficient and highly accurate method for calculating Newtonian potentials based on boundary elements, specifically suitable for unbounded and partially bounded two-dimensional domains. The method leverages high-order approximations and advanced quadrature techniques to minimize errors and computational time. In our tests, we compared this method with a traditional volume-based approach using a grid without a set pattern for different types of domains and found it to be significantly faster and more accurate.
